answer:
That name is read inside-out, one layer per feature that touched the face:

1. **`base.outline.bottom`** — the origin: an entity of the sketch `base`. Your sketch (script.js) draws `.rect('outline', 'w', 'd', { center: true })`, and a rectangle is four lines; the one at y = −d/2 is `outline.bottom`. The compiler tags the edge of the extrusion that came from that line, so the side wall of the box inherits the sketch entity that generated it.

2. **`body/side[base.outline.bottom]`** — the extrude feature `body` swept that profile to height 30 mm. Each vertical wall is a side face produced by one profile edge, so it's named `body/side[<source entity>]`. Four walls: `…bottom`, `…top`, `…left`, `…right` — you can see them with [faces](lab:face?name=body/side%5Bbase.outline.bottom%5D) or `faces('body/side*')`.

3. **`shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`** — the shell feature hollowed the box, offsetting each wall inward. The inner wall it created is *derived from* the outer wall, so the outer face's whole name is embedded in brackets as the provenance: "the inner face that shell made from body's side wall that came from the sketch's bottom outline line."

The point of the scheme is that names survive edits by recording **history, not coordinates**. If you later change `w` or `d` in [params](lab:show?view=params), or fillet the corners above the shell, the bottom wall is still the face swept from `base.outline.bottom`, so `j.feat('shell').faces('inner')` keeps resolving to it — no index-based `nth()` fragility. If a later feature splits that wall, the pieces keep the name with a suffix (`#a`, `#b`). `why('…')` on any such name prints exactly this chain, each link saying which feature created the face and from what.

No — the outline sketch is **under-constrained by exactly 1 DOF**, and the solver names it precisely.

## The numbers

The solver's ledger for `outline` ([sketch record](lab:node?id=outline)):

- **Entity DOF Σ = 22**: each line has 4 DOF (two endpoints × x, y) → 4 lines = 16; each circle has 3 DOF (center x, y, radius) → 2 circles = 6.
- **Constraint rank = 21**: the 4 coincidences (8 equations), fix (2), 2 horizontals + 2 verticals (4), equal (1), two lengths (2), diameter (1), three distance dims (3) — all independent.
- **DOF = 22 − 21 = 1**, status `under`, one cluster, dogleg converged with residual 0 in 1 iteration.

## What's free

The only free coordinate is **`h2.center.x`** (`dofFree: [center.x]` on h2). Everything else is locked:

- The rectangle: `fix(l1.start)` anchors it, h/v constraints square it, and `length(l1) = w = 80 mm`, `length(l2) = d = 40 mm` size it — the four coincidences close the loop.
- `h1`: diameter = `hole_d`, placed by `distanceX = edge = 12 mm` and `distanceY = d/2 = 20 mm` from the fixed corner — 0 DOF.
- `h2`: shares h1's size via `equal(h2, h1)` and its height via `distanceY(h1.center, h2.center) = 0` — that leaves only the horizontal position free.

This is intentional ([script.js:4–6](lab:open?file=script.js&line=4)): h2 is the drag hole. If you ever want it fully constrained, one more equation at rank 22 would do — e.g. `dim({ h: ['h1.center', 'h2.center'] }, 'w - 2 * edge')`, which would make DOF = 22 − 22 = 0 and the diagnostic disappear. As it stands, the warning `sketch.underConstrained` (1 DOF, at line 35) is exactly the affordance letting you drag h2 along x.

answer:
**On its side — with the side profile lying flat on the bed** (the compiler chose −Y, symmetric with +Y, in `program.decisions()` under `orient`).

Why this is the right way up for this part:

- **Zero support, everything bridging-free.** The whole side outline (18 × 35 mm) touches the bed as one face (240 mm²), so every layer is a closed loop — no overhangs at all (`overhangArea: 0`, `supportVolume: 0`). Any other axis is worse: lying flat on the desk-face (+X) needs 134 mm³ of support under the jaw lead-ins, and printing standing up (±Z) needs ~1.5 cm³ of support inside the C-shaped jaws and channel.
- **Layer lines reinforce the flex.** This is the part of the clip that actually bends — the jaws spring over the desk edge when you push it on. With the profile on the bed, the extrusion lines run along the length of the jaws and spine, so the bending loads pull along filaments instead of peeling layers apart (the comment on [script.js:56](lab:open?file=script.js&line=56) says exactly this).
- **Height is only 12 mm** (the clip width `w`), 60 layers at 0.2 mm — short, stable, no brim-worthy footprint issues.

The two side-lying orientations (±Y) tie exactly, which is fine since the profile is symmetric about the bed plane. If you ever print a long run of these (`qty` > 1), ±X packing could fit more per plate, but I'd keep the side-down orientation and eat the bed area — the layer orientation is worth more than packing density on a 12-minute part.

One full turn moves the rack by the pinion's **pitch circumference**:

- Module $m = 2$ mm, 18 teeth → pitch radius $r = \frac{m z}{2} = \frac{2 \times 18}{2} = 18$ mm
- Travel per turn $= 2\pi r = \pi m z = 2\pi \times 18 \approx \mathbf{113.10\ mm}$

That's the note in [notes.md line 11](lab:open?file=notes.md&line=11), and it's the coupling rule from the brief: whenever you set both joints, rack travel = pitch radius × angle in radians, so $113.10$ mm per turn. (The rack itself only has 16 teeth = 64 mm of toothed length, so the full stroke isn't achievable without the pinion running off the end.)

answer:
The hinge uses the **`printInPlace` fit class: 0.4 mm per side** (so 0.8 mm total across the joint). That's set in the script in two places, both on `j.fit.gap('printInPlace')`:

- **script.js:12–13** — `j.lib.hinge.pin({ knuckles: n, length: mm(L), d: mm(d), clearance: 'printInPlace', wall: mm(1.6) })`, which bores the even knuckles at the pin diameter $3 + 2 \times 0.4 = 3.8$ mm and sizes the knuckle radius $R = 1.5 + 0.4 + 1.6 = 3.5$ mm.
- **script.js:66** — `.printInPlace(['base', 'lid'], { clearance: mm(c), ... })`, with `c = 0.4` from line 10, so the assembly-level gap check uses the same number.

**Calibration: no.** The `gap.*` params all come from `src: default fit classes (uncalibrated)` — `gap.printInPlace` is the stock 0.4 mm, not a value measured on your printer. Nothing in the script calls `j.fit.profile(...)` with a calibrated profile or `j.fit.calibrate(...)` with measured outcomes, so the 0.4 mm is a conservative default, not a tuned one.

If you want it tuned, the path is: print `j.fit.coupon({ kind: 'pin-hole', steps: 10 })` on your printer, measure which gap actually spins freely, and feed the results into `j.fit.calibrate([...])` — that produces a profile like `j.fit.profile('mk4-pla', { classes: { printInPlace: mm(0.32) } })` you could add to the parts. A tighter calibrated gap would let you shrink `c` and the stand-off `off = R + c`, closing the box a little. Worth noting the pin/knuckle clearance is the load-bearing number here: too tight and the hinge fuses, and the coupon only tests a plain pin-hole pair, so re-check the assembled hinge after any change (the `.printInPlace()` check at several poses, per your brief, is the guard).

answer:
From the front (the sketch plane, XZ) the outline is a tall, open **C-shaped hook** — one closed profile of eighteen segments, extruded 12 mm wide. Reading it the way the clip is used, with the desk filling x ≥ 0 between z = 0 and z = `desk` (18 mm):

- **The spine** — the vertical wall at x = −`t` on the left. It's the back of the part, joining the two jaws; its thickness `t` (3 mm) is the wall that everything hangs from.
- **The top jaw** — the arm reaching right, over the desk's top face at z = `desk`. It ends at x = `jaw` (15 mm) with a small **grip bump** on its underside (`desk − grip` at `jaw − 2 mm`): a 0.6 mm rise that pinches the board's underside so the clip doesn't slide off. In front of it, the short slope from `jaw` up to `desk + 1 mm` is the **lead-in** — it spreads the jaw as you push the clip on.
- **The bottom jaw** — the mirror image under the desk: outer face at z = −`t`, tip at x = `jaw`, with its own bump (`grip` up from z = 0) and its own lead-in slope below it. The two bumps together give the 0.4–0.8 mm grip range.
- **The cable channel** — the rectangular pocket cut into the bottom of the hook, between the two jaws: bounded by the lip at x = `cable + t` and the floor at z = −`t − cable`, so the channel is `cable` (8 mm) wide. A cable pushed up into it is held in the open slot under the desk; the small stepped lip (`cable + t` up to `−t − cable/2`) keeps the cable from sliding back out.

So functionally it's a spring clip: spine = structure, two jaws = clamps, bumps = retention, slopes = assembly lead-ins, channel = cable holder. Everything is written in the six params, which is why changing `desk` moves the jaws without touching the channel. You can see the profile as drawn at [front view](lab:view?name=front), or inspect the desk-face at [body/side[side.outline.14]](lab:face?name=body/side[side.outline.14]).

The hole is placed at the floor plane, but the box was extruded **upward** from XY, so the cut goes down into empty space — that's the `feature.noEffect` warning. Let me confirm the option to flip it:

The real problem: the hole at `[45, 0]` is **outside the box** (outer edge is at x = 30 mm, since w = 60), so the cut misses every body. And a bare point needs anchoring to a face for the hole to register. Let me find the floor face and test the fix:

**Done — the hole is fixed and the script compiles clean.**

**What was wrong (two things):**

1. **The hole was outside the part.** Your mount point was at `[45, 0]`, but the box's outside width is $w = 60$ mm centred on the origin, so the outer wall is at $x = 30$ mm. A point at x = 45 is 15 mm beyond the wall, so the cut missed every body entirely — that's exactly what the `feature.noEffect` warning ("the cut removes no material, it misses every body") was telling you. My first guess (that the direction was wrong, since the box extrudes up from XY and the hole cuts down from the floor) turned out not to be it: I tested `dir: '+Z'`, `'-Z'`, `'+X'` and a bare `[45, 0, 30]` point in the sandbox, and every variant still warned `feature.noEffect`.

2. **A bare point doesn't anchor.** Even with the x-coordinate corrected, a plain `[20, 0]` point produced the same no-effect warning. Anchoring the point to the floor face fixed it.

**The fix (script.js, last line, replaced in place):**

```js
.hole([j.point.on(j.feat('body').startFace(), { at: [20, 0] })], j.hole.simple(mm(5), 'through'), { id: 'mount' })
```

`j.feat('body').startFace()` is the floor (the XY face the box was extruded from), and `[20, 0]` puts the hole 20 mm right of centre in sketch coordinates, as you intended. `j.point.on(face, { at })` anchors the point on that face so the "through" bore actually lands in material.

**What I verified:**

- Before: volume 15344.265 mm³, 19 faces, warning `feature.noEffect` at mount.
- Sandbox variant with the fix: volume 15304.996 mm³ (39.27 mm³ removed ≈ $\pi \cdot 2.5^2 \cdot 2$ through a 2 mm floor — checks out exactly), **no warnings**, and the B-rep gained a cylinder face named `mount/bore[1]`.
- After editing script.js and running `run()` on the open workbench: `ok: true`, warnings: `[]`.

Note the volume differs slightly from the sandbox figure I quoted (15305 vs the earlier 15344−39) — both are the same cut; the small difference is the outer-corner fillets in the real script vs the plain test box in my first sandbox probes.

**Unfinished / suggestions:**

- I didn't draw the result (`look()`), so you haven't seen it visually — the face name `mount/bore[1]` and the exact volume delta confirm it, but a quick look from the plan view would show the hole sitting 20 mm right of centre on the floor.
- The hole position is a hard-coded `[20, 0]` rather than a param. If you want it adjustable in Params, I can add e.g. `mount_x: mm(20)` and use that — say the word.
- The diagnostic suggested "a cut from a sketch plane goes along the plane normal" — worth remembering: `.hole()` cuts along the point's face normal, so anchoring on the floor is also what gives the correct through-direction here.

answer:
A face name in jig is a genealogy: `<feature>/<role>[<source>]`, read outwards-in. So `shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]` is three layers, each naming the feature that made the face, the role it played there, and (in brackets) what it came from.

- **`base.outline.bottom`** — the innermost layer is a sketch entity of the sketch `base` ([line 19](lab:open?file=script.js&line=19)): `rect('outline', 'w', 'd', …)` creates sides `outline.bottom right top left` and corners `outline.bl br tr tl`. This is the *bottom* side, i.e. the one at $-Y$.
- **`body/side[...]`** — the `body` extrude sweeps each profile curve into a face; a lateral (swept) face gets the role `side` and records the sketch curve it was swept from. `start`/`end` are the two caps. So `body/side[base.outline.bottom]` is the outer wall on the $-Y$ side.
- **`shell/inner[...]`** — the `shell` feature offsets the open face's neighbours inward; the new cavity wall gets the role `inner` and records the face it was offset from. Hence the whole string, and [`why`](lab:open?file=script.js&line=25) prints exactly that chain: `shell/inner[…] ← shell: offset of body/side[…]; body/side[…] ← body: swept from sketch entity base.outline.bottom`.

The face itself is the flat middle of the box's inner $-Y$ wall: normal $+Y$ (into the cavity), centre $(0,-18,16)$, area $1512 = 54 \times 28\ \text{mm}^2$ — inner width $w-2\cdot\text{wall}=56$ minus $2\times1$ mm of corner radius, times cavity depth $h-\text{wall}=28$. The rounded corners of the rect ($r=3$) are why this face is not the whole side: the corners are separate cylinders `shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bl]]` and `[…br]`, radius $1\ \text{mm} = r - \text{wall}$, area $43.98\ \text{mm}^2$ each.

The payoff is that the name states intent, not an index: at `wall = 2.5 mm` (a `check()` variant) the same face keeps the same name and becomes $54 \times 27.5 = 1485\ \text{mm}^2$ with centre $(0,-17.5,16.25)$ — a `.nth(i)` reference would have been meaningless. Push `wall` to 3 mm and the shell fails (`feature.failed`, "could not offset the faces", line 25) because the inner corner radius would be $r-\text{wall}=0$; the *name* is robust, the geometry that has to exist for it is not.

answer:
It prints **on its side**: the build direction is −Y, so the side profile (the XZ outline) is the first layer and the layers stack across the clip's 12 mm width — 60 layers at 0.2 mm.

That came from the automatic orientation (`orient('auto')`, the default), not from anything in the script — see the `orient` decision in the trace:

| direction | support | bed contact | height |
|---|---|---|---|
| **−Y** (chosen) | 0 mm³ | 240.4 mm² | 12 mm |
| +Y | 0 mm³ | 240.4 mm² | 12 mm |
| +X | 134.4 mm³ | 420 mm² | 18 mm |
| ±Z (upright) | 1451–1510 mm³ | 168–216 mm² | 35 mm |
| −X | 1638 mm³ | 48 mm² | 18 mm |

The rule is lexicographic: least support volume first, then most bed contact, then least height. ±Y and +Y are geometrically identical (the two side faces `body/start` and `body/end` are both 240.4 mm², and the whole outline lands flat), so the tie falls to the first candidate tried. The tempting wrong answer is +X, which has more bed contact (420 mm²) but would need 134 mm³ of support — support outranks contact. Upright would be 35 mm tall (the $desk + t$ top jaw plus the $2t + cable$ hook) with about 1.5 cm³ of unsupported jaw and lip.

The result is a zero-overhang print (`overhang: []`, `supportVolume: 0`), and the right one for the part: the jaws flex across the desk thickness — in $z$ — which is inside the layer plane, so the flexing jaw is not loaded across layer lines. It is why [notes.md](lab:open?file=notes.md&find=lays%20the%20clip%20on%20its%20side) calls this out as the strong direction.

Worth knowing: this is a property of the shape, not of the parameters. Widen the clip much ($w$ above roughly the 18 × 35 mm footprint's short side) or shrink $desk$ far enough and ±Y can stop winning on bed contact — the decision is recomputed on every compile, so [changing `w`](lab:param?name=w&value=30%20mm) and reading the decision again is the honest check.

answer:
**Answer: ≈ 0.203 mm** — the pinion–wheel gap as reported by the assembly's interference check (the "pinion–wheel" gap decision in the open program).

What backs it up, and its world:

- The interference pass in `script.js` (`.interference()` at the end of the `pair` assembly) runs on the **display meshes**, not the B-rep. The decision reads `pinion–wheel · gap · ≈ 0.203 mm`, with the reason string *"minimum distance between components (display meshes; { exact: true } for the B-rep distance)"*. So this is an **approximate** number: the compiled L6 mesh report gives meshing deflections of 0.057 mm (pinion) and 0.108 mm (wheel), so a few hundredths of a millimetre of slack in that last digit is plausible.
- The rest of the mesh check, from `j.inspect.gearMesh(pinion, wheel)` at the script's own value: centre distance 54 mm (= m(z₁+z₂)/2, not typed), ratio 2, working pressure 20°, **contact ratio 1.61**, **backlash 0.4 mm** (free-class thinning), `ok: true`, no messages. The other two gaps are base–pinion and base–wheel, both ≈ 0.200 mm (the spacer clearance).
- The `notes.md` and the script's comment say the wheel joint starts at 5° (= 180°/36, half a tooth), which is why a pinion tooth sits in a wheel gap and the minimum clearance is tooth-flank-to-tooth-flank rather than a crash.

Unfinished: I tried to get the **exact B-rep distance** by recompiling a variant with `.interference({ exact: true })`, but the decision text came back unchanged (still "display meshes") — that option doesn't appear to be honoured in this build, and `j.inspect.distance` on two gears gives 0 mm (they share a coordinate origin, so it's not a part-to-part measure). I also started a mesh-level STL cross-check of the pinion and wheel triangle sets but hit a buffer-offset error in my parser; that would only confirm the mesh figure, not turn it into an exact one. If you want a trustworthy exact value, the clean route is a direct B-rep minimum-distance query between the two assembled bodies, which I couldn't reach from here — I'd need to know whether the `exact` flag is meant to be supported, since it silently isn't.

answer:
**113.10 mm** — one full turn of the pinion advances the rack by its pitch circumference.

The pinion in [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=6) is `module 2 mm, teeth 18`, so its pitch radius is $r = m z / 2 = 18$ mm. One turn is $2\pi$ rad, and the coupling rule in the notes (`travel = r × angle`) gives

$$\text{travel} = r\theta = 18 \times 2\pi = 113.097\ \text{mm}.$$

The same number comes out of the mesh inspection both ways: `j.inspect.gearMesh(pinion, rack)` reports `travelPerTurn: 113.09734` and `pitchLineDistance: 18 mm` (from a `check()` compile — the same values the open program's `mesh` uses for `yc`), and it equals 18 teeth × the circular pitch $\pi m = 6.2832$ mm.

One design note while we're on the number: the rack is `teeth: 16`, i.e. $16\pi m = 100.53$ mm of toothed length. A full turn is longer than the rack itself, so past about **0.889 turn (320°)** the pinion's last tooth would run off the end of the rack — if you want a full crank revolution to stay in mesh, the rack needs 18 or more teeth (or `travel` must be limited to 100.5 mm, $\theta \le 320°$).

answer:
The hinge runs on the **print-in-place fit class**, and no — that fit is not calibrated for any printer in this script.

**What clearance it uses.** The `j.lib.hinge.pin(...)` call at [line 25](lab:open?file=script.js&line=25) sets `clearance: 'printInPlace'`, which is `j.fit.gap('printInPlace')` = **0.40 mm per side**. Measured off the compiled B-rep, the pin face `hinge/pin#a` has radius **1.50 mm (Ø3.0)** and the lid-side knuckle bores `hinge/bore2` / `hinge/bore4` are radius **1.90 mm (Ø3.8)** — so Ø3.8 bore on a Ø3.0 pin gives exactly Ø0.8 / **0.40 mm radial** running clearance, matching the comment on [line 18](lab:open?file=script.js&line=18). The pin is kept at nominal and the bore carries the whole allowance.

**Is it calibrated?** No. All five fit classes read `src: "default fit classes (uncalibrated)"`:

| class | gap/side |
|---|---|
| press | 0.05 mm |
| snug | 0.10 mm |
| slide | 0.20 mm |
| free | 0.30 mm |
| printInPlace | **0.40 mm** |

There is no `.fit(j.fit.profile('…'))` call anywhere in [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js) (grep for `.fit(` finds none), no `j.fit.calibrate(…)`, and the script's own defaults flow straight through. So the 0.4 mm is the library's generic PLA/PETG starting point, not a value measured from your machine's over/under-extrusion. In this build the expected `fit.uncalibrated` info diagnostic is also silent, so nothing warns you at runtime — the "uncalibrated" provenance on the `gap.printInPlace` param is your only signal.

**If a pin this free binds on your printer** (or rattles), the calibrated route is a profile — e.g. `.fit(j.fit.profile('mk4-petg', { classes: { printInPlace: mm(0.30) } }))` near [line 24](lab:open?file=script.js&line=24) — or a print-in-place test coupon from `j.fit.coupon({ kind: 'pin-hole', steps: 10 })` to find your real per-side gap first. I'd want your printer/material before picking a number; want me to draft that edit?

I'll start by looking at the script and the failing area.



Fixed: the sketch had two dimensions on the same line, `.dim('l1', 'w')` (= 80 mm) and a leftover `.dim('l1', 90)`. I deleted the stray one — script.js line 22 is now `j.c.dim('l1','w')` … the 90 line is gone, so [open script.js:20](lab:open?file=script.js&line=20) shows only the param-driven dimensions.

**Why it failed, in solver terms.** The outline has 4 lines (4 DOF each) and 2 circles (3 each): $\sum \text{DOF}_{\text{ent}} = 16 + 6 = 22$. The constraint set is 16 rows — 4 implicit coincidences (2 each), `fix(l1.start)` (2), 2 horizontal + 2 vertical (4), `equal(h2,h1)` (1), and 6 dimension rows (two lengths, one diameter, distanceX, two distanceY). The Jacobian of those 16 rows has rank 21, so $\text{DOF} = 22 - 21 = 1$, with `h2` free in `center.x` — exactly the drag handle the brief wants. The extra `length(l1) = 90 mm` was a 17th row whose gradient is the same as `length(l1) = 80 mm` (dependent), so it could not raise the rank; instead it made the residual vector inconsistent and the solver reported `sketch.overConstrained` with the minimal conflicting set `{80 mm, 90 mm}`.

**After the fix** (`run()` from the open program, exact B-rep): `ok: true`, sketch status `under`, DOF **1**, free entity `h2 (1: center.x)`, no errors, one expected `sketch.underConstrained` warning. Body: volume 12672.765 mm³, mass 15.714 g, bbox 80 × 40 × 4 mm.

Two checks that the diagnosis is right: keeping the 90 as a *driven* reference (`{ driven: true }`) also compiles with DOF 1 — it is a measurement, not a constraint, so it adds no rank; and starting `h2` at `[50, 20]` compiles with DOF 1 unchanged and h2 centre.x sitting at 50, confirming that coordinate is genuinely free rather than pinned. Keep `w` at 80 mm as the only width authority — if you ever want a 90 mm plate, change the param instead: [param w = 90 mm](lab:param?name=w&value=90%20mm).

answer:
**What you see** — one flat C-shaped outline, 18 mm deep × 35 mm tall, with a hook hanging under its lower jaw; extruded 12 mm along the desk edge ([front view](lab:view?name=front), sketch at [script.js:7](lab:open?file=script.js&line=7)). It reads as three functional zones: a **spine** down the back, two **jaws** that clamp the board, and a **cable cup** under the bottom jaw. Every vertex is an expression of `desk, cable, t, jaw, grip` ([script.js:31](lab:open?file=script.js&line=31)); at the script's values the points land on round numbers.

Tracing the closed polyline from the top jaw tip:

- **Top jaw, upper edge** — `(15, 21) → (−3, 21)`: a flat 3 mm-thick arm (`t`) reaching `jaw` = 15 mm onto the board; it swallows the spine at x = −3.
- **Spine** — `(−3, 21) → (−3, −14)`: one straight back face, 35 mm, serving the top jaw, the board slot and the cable cup at once. It is the outermost surface you see when the clip is on.
- **Hook base and lip** — `(−3, −14) → (11, −14) → (11, −7) → (8, −7) → (8, −11) → (0, −11)`: the bottom of the hook is a 3 mm floor at z = −14; at its outer end a 3 mm wall (`x 8…11`) rises to z = −7, i.e. `cable/2` = 4 mm above the floor. That stubby post is the **lip**: with the channel floor and the jaw underside it makes a `cable × cable` = 8 × 8 mm pocket with only a **4 mm mouth**, so a cable is pressed in over the lip and stays caught.
- **Channel back** — `(0, −11) → (0, −3)`: a wall flush with the board's edge plane, closing the pocket on the desk side.
- **Bottom jaw** — `(0, −3) → (15, −3)` then up the jaw tip `(15, −1)` and the ramp `(13, 0.6) → (11, 0) → (0, 0)`: 3 mm of arm under the board, thickening where the **grip bump** at x = 13 stands `grip` = 0.6 mm proud of the board line, with a shallow 2 mm **lead-in** ahead of it down to 1 mm clearance at the tip — the pair that spreads the jaw as you push it on.
- **Board slot** — `(0, 0) → (0, 18) → (11, 18) → (13, 17.4) → (15, 19)`: the `desk` × `jaw`-deep gap the board enters, closed by the flat edge face at x = 0 (that face is the datum everything hangs off: `body/side[side.outline.14]`), then the mirrored top-jaw bump and lead-in, and the tip face `(15, 19) → (15, 21)`.

Two things worth noting in the drawing: the two jaw tips are **not** the same thickness (the bottom jaw carries grip + lead-in, so it is ~4 mm at the tip), and the 18 mm dimension under the profile is `t + jaw`, the outline's own depth — not the desk thickness, which is the 18 mm gap inside it. Everything is 2 mm-plus walls at the default `t` = 3 (the tightest span, `jaw − 4 mm` to `jaw − 2 mm`, is the bump, which is intentional pinch, not wall).

```js
logo_text: j.lit('JIG'), logo_size: mm(10), logo_depth: mm(0.6),
...
.emboss(
  j.region.text('JIG', { size: 'logo_size' }), 'logo_depth',
  { on: j.sel.faces('-Y').of('body').largest(), op: 'cut', id: 'logo' })
```

It cuts 0.6 mm into the 2 mm wall on the **outside** of the −Y face — `j.sel.faces('-Y').of('body').largest()` is `body/side[base.outline.bottom]` (area 1620 mm², normal −Y), *not* the inner shell face, which also has a −Y normal. The engraving floors sit at $y=-19.4$, i.e. exactly 0.6 mm in from $y=-20$, so the cut is right and the wall keeps 1.4 mm behind it.

The front view ([view](lab:view?name=front)) and the axo both show the three glyphs on the outside of the near face.

**Does it read left to right?** Yes. In the front elevation, viewed from outside (−Y looking toward +Y with +Z up), the letters appear in the order J-I-G with the J on the left and G on the right — the same order as the string, not mirrored. The dimension/axes convention holds because the sketch's local +X maps to world +X on that face, which is what you see going left-to-right from the front.

**One loose end:** I declared a `logo_text: j.lit('JIG')` param but the emboss still uses the literal string — `j.region.text` does not take the text from a param by name (passing a param there engraved the name, not its value).
```js
// U-0x · Cat magnet pin: a flat cat head with a press-fit magnet pocket
// in its back. The head is one silhouette (a circle plus two ears), given
// thickness; the magnet pocket is cut into the back and stops short of the
// face, so the disc magnet seats flush and never shows through.

// silhouette: a head circle plus two triangular ears, all driven by `r`
const P  = a => [`r * cos(${a} deg)`, `r * sin(${a} deg)`];     // point on head circle
const TP = (a, k) => [`${k} * r * cos(${a} deg)`, `${k} * r * sin(${a} deg)`]; // ear tip
const head = j.region.circle('r')
  .union(j.region.polygon([P(102), P(148), TP(124, '1.42')]))   // left ear
  .union(j.region.polygon([P(78),  P(32),  TP(56,  '1.42')]));  // right ear

const pin = j.part('cat-magnet-pin')
  .params({
    w: mm(30),          // head width across the cheeks
    t: mm(4),           // thickness
    r: 'w / 2',         // head radius
    mag_d: mm(10),      // disc magnet diameter
    mag_h: mm(2),       // disc magnet thickness -> pocket depth
  })
  // three sizes; the middle row (standard) is active by default
  .configs({
    petite:  { w: mm(24), mag_d: mm(8) },
    standard: { w: mm(30), mag_d: mm(10) },
    grande:  { w: mm(40), mag_d: mm(12) },
  })
  .expose(['w', 't', 'mag_d', 'mag_h'], {
    labels: { w: 'head width', t: 'thickness', mag_d: 'magnet diameter', mag_h: 'magnet thickness' },
    ranges: { w: [mm(20), mm(50)], t: [mm(3.5), mm(6)], mag_d: [mm(5), mm(15)], mag_h: [mm(1), mm(3)] },
  })
  .extrude(head, 't', { id: 'body' })
  // press-fit pocket in the back (top face), cut down to `mag_h` plus a little
  // clearance: with t = 4 the floor stays about 1.8 mm, so it never breaks through
  .add(j.lib.magnet({ d: 'mag_d', h: 'mag_h' }),
       { at: j.frame.on(j.feat('body').endFace()), id: 'mag' });

return j.print('cat-magnet-pin', {
  printer: j.printer('generic-fdm'), material: j.material('PLA'),
  parts: [pin],
}).orient('+Z');   // front (cat face) down, pocket opening up: no support
```
